newsitem.title: ISRAEL: Appointment of new Bezeq chief blocked.
newsitem.headline: Appointment of new Bezeq chief blocked.

text.p: Israel's main telecommunications carrier, state-owned Bezeq Israel Telecom, was left without a managing director on Monday after a watchdog committee froze the appointment of the man named to the post.

The public committee, which examines possible conflicts of interest for civil servants, ruled on Sunday that Yoram Turbowicz, former director of the government's anti-trust authority, would have to wait a year before taking up the top job at Bezeq.
He had been due to take over on Sunday from Yitzhak Kaul, who has now left the company to become managing director of Clal Israel Ltd.
The committee found a potential conflict of interest in that Turbowicz dealt with Bezeq affairs in his previous anti-trust job.
The decision caught the government by surprise.

"Up until now, the committee had never refused to shorten the cooling off period in the case of a transfer from one government job to a post in a state-owned company," the Communications Ministry said in a statement.
Bezeq is 76 percent state-owned, although it plans to reduce the stake this year, probably through a domestic public offering.
A ministry spokeswoman said no interim managing director for Bezeq had yet been named and that officials were meeting now to discuss what to do next.
Turbowicz has made no public comment about the committee's decision.

Later this year Bezeq will face competition in its hugely profitable international phone service business. The government has awarded licences to two international consortiums to offer competing service.

Bezeq also faces more competition in its cellular business as the government plans to publish a tender for a third operator by July. Further down the line, the government aims to open basic and interurban telephone service as well as telecommunications infrastructure to competition by the end of 1998.

Cable & Wireless PLC bought 10 percent of Bezeq in the stock market two years ago, to the government's chagrin and the two sides are in talks over what the British company's role will be in the planned public sell-off.
